props.title: The Shining
props.initialSlug: Kubrick's horror classic featuring alcoholism as subtext
props.initialStreaming: Max, Max Amazon Channel, Cinemax Amazon Channel

sections.content: The Shining revolutionized psychological horror through Kubrick's masterful manipulation of space and symmetry. The Overlook Hotel becomes a character itself, with Danny's Big Wheel sequences and impossible window placement creating deep unease. Kubrick departed significantly from Stephen King's novel, focusing less on supernatural elements and more on Jack's psychological deterioration. The film's influence echoes through modern horror like The Babadook (2014) and Hereditary (2018), which similarly explore family dynamics crumbling under supernatural pressure.

sections.content: Kubrick's obsessive attention to detail resulted in the Guinness World Record for most takes of a single scene - 127 takes of Shelley Duvall backing up the stairs. The film's innovative use of the Steadicam, then a new technology, created the eerily smooth tracking shots that became horror cinema language. Halloween (1978) had used similar techniques, but The Shining perfected fluid camera movement as a tool for building dread.

The film's ambiguous ending continues generating debate decades later. Unlike later horror films that explain everything, Kubrick leaves crucial questions unanswered: the meaning of the final photograph, whether the hotel is truly haunted or Jack is simply mad, and the nature of Danny's "shining" ability. This influenced enigmatic horror like The Witch (2015) and It Follows (2014). SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation and Visual Language

sections.content: The Shining's visual symmetry and one-point perspective shots created a template for horror cinematography. Every frame is meticulously composed - the twins in the hallway, the hexagonal carpet patterns, the mirror images throughout. Modern films like Us (2019) and Midsommar (2019) directly reference this visual language. The famous "Here's Johnny!" scene pioneered the use of extreme close-ups in horror, while the river of blood sequence remains one of cinema's most memorable practical effects.
